However, this collapses under Popper's own strictures because without a probabilistic assumption that nature is uniform (i.e., that the future will resemble the past), there is no rational basis to assume a theory with high verisimilitude today will remain successful or 'closer to truth' in future applications. By asserting that surviving severe tests makes a theory the 'best approximation' for action, the target implicitly smuggles in the very inductive principle Popper rejected: that past performance is a reliable guide to future utility. If one cannot assign a higher probability of success to the corroborated theory, the preference becomes arbitrary, not rational; if one can, one has reintroduced induction.", "outcome": "raised and not answered; the target's status did not move"}
